questions.title: What is the precise mathematical definition of Hyperspherical Energy, and why is minimizing its difference to the pretrained model considered a guarantee of semantic preservation?
questions.question_body: I am reading Section 3.1 (General Framework) where the paper defines Hyperspherical Energy (HE) as $\text{HE}(\bm{W}):= \sum_{i\neq j} \\|\hat{\\bm{w}}_i-\hat{\\bm{w}}_j|^{-1}$, where $\hat{\\bm{w}}_i$ are normalized neurons. I understand that OFT aims to make $\|\text{HE}(\\bm{W})-\text{HE}(\\bm{W}^0)\\\|=0$. However, I am struggling to connect this abstract geometric property to the actual 'semantic generation ability' mentioned in the abstract. The paper states that HE captures 'pairwise neuron relationship on the unit hypersphere' and that angle differences encode semantic information. Could someone derive or explain *why* preserving this specific sum of inverse distances between normalized vectors mathematically guarantees that the model's ability to generate text-conditioned images is preserved, rather than just being a regularization trick?

questions.title: Can you clarify the exact relationship between Cayley Parameterization, block-diagonal matrices, and the determinant constraint in OFT?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2 (Efficient Orthogonal Parameterization), the paper introduces CIF parameterization: $\\bm{R}=(\\bm{I}+\\bm{Q})(I-\\bm{Q})^{-1}$ where $\\bm{Q}$ is skew-symmetric. It mentions this yields matrices with determinant 1 (Special Orthogonal Group). Later, it introduces block-diagonal matrices with $r$ blocks and claims this allows utilizing full orthogonal matrices while maintaining efficiency. Is there a conflict here? Does using block-diagonal matrices with Cayley parameterization allow us to reach determinants of -1 (reflections), or are we still restricted to rotations only? The paper says 'such a limitation does not affect performance', but from a theoretical standpoint for diffusion models where direction matters (up to sign), how does using only SO(d) vs O(d) impact the finetuning capability?

questions.title: How do we compare parameter efficiency between OFT and LoRA without fixing hyperparameters like alpha or rank?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2, Table 1 (LSN dummy name) shows an example comparing LoRA and OFT for a 128x128 layer: LoRA with r=8 has 2048 params (rank r times d + n), while OFT with r=8 has 960 params ($d * d / r^2$). Since standard practice uses $r = alpha * d$ for LoRA where alpha can be small like 0.0625 or large like 32, how should we fairly compare them if we vary alpha? If I set LoRA's alpha = 4, it would have huge params compared to fixed d/r=16 for OFT. Does this comparison implicitly assume specific lower bounds or upper bounds on ratio r/d for both methods?

questions.title: Does Rescaled Orthogonal Finetuning introduce any new constraints on hyperspherical energy, or does it truly preserve it by construction?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.4 (Re-scaled OFT), they add a diagonal matrix D to finetune magnitudes via forward pass: z = ([bold R W0 D]) transpose x. They claim re-scaling neurons does not change HE because magnitude gets normalized out during cosine similarity calculations in HE definition. However, if D is learnable and independent across neurons during backpropagation, does this introduce non-orthogonal deformations that might occasionally push weights off-unit hypersphere temporarily before normalization? Or is HE defined strictly as sum of inverse distances ONLY ON unit hypersphere at prediction time insensible to pre-normalization intermediate values?
